```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Formatting helpers local to this manuscript. `pc` prints a percentage the
# way the journal sets them; `cnt` a count with thousands separators.
# The cohort denominators, taken from the catalog where it carries them and
# from the frozen linkage manifest otherwise, never typed.
# Named exactly as build_stats_catalog.R defines them: `total` is
# certification records, `matched` is those resolving to a provider record,
# and `cohort_n` is the live analytic cohort including the nursing-taxonomy
# sensitivity tier.
linkage_total_n <- K$linkage$total
linkage_matched_n <- K$linkage$matched
linkage_matched_pct <- K$linkage$matched_pct
cohort_n <- K$linkage$cohort_n

n_word <- function(x) {
  words <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight",
             "nine", "ten", "eleven", "twelve")
  if (is.null(x) || is.na(x)) "**[PENDING]**" else
    if (x >= 1 && x <= length(words)) words[x] else as.character(x)
}

# A NUMBER WORD AT THE START OF A SENTENCE IS STILL THE START OF A SENTENCE.
# n_word() returns lower case because most uses are mid-sentence, and two uses
# in Materials and Methods were not: the rendered manuscript opened sentences
# with "eleven record systems were examined" and "nine sources were compared".
# Capitalizing at the call site is what a copy editor would otherwise do by
# hand on every render.
N_word <- function(x) sub("^(.)", "\\U\\1", n_word(x), perl = TRUE)

pc  <- function(x, d = 1) if (is.null(x) || is.na(x)) "**[PENDING]**" else
  sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), x)
cnt <- function(x) if (is.null(x) || is.na(x)) "**[PENDING]**" else
  formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
```

**Précis:** Federal provider databases describing certified nurse-midwives are
accurate for licensure status but disagree with one another about practice
location, and most disagreements never resolve.

## Abstract

**OBJECTIVE:** To examine the accuracy, completeness, and internal
consistency of publicly available databases describing the United States
certified nurse-midwife workforce, and to determine which variables can
support geographic research.

**METHODS:** We replicated the 2013 Office of Inspector General evaluation
of federal provider data [@oig2013] for a national cohort of certified
nurse-midwives drawn from the American Midwifery Certification Board roster
and linked to the National Plan and Provider Enumeration System. Accuracy
was assessed against two independent primary sources: state board of
nursing licensure verification and the certification board roster.
Completeness was the proportion of eligible records carrying a value.
Consistency was pairwise disagreement between databases describing the
same provider in the same year, across `r n_word(A$sources_total_n)` record
systems.

**RESULTS:** Where an independent primary source existed, records were
largely accurate: licensure status in the national provider registry agreed
with live state board verification for
`r pc(A$nppes_license_3$pct_accurate, 2)` of resolved records in three
machine-verified states and `r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_accurate, 2)`
across seven. Of inaccurate records,
`r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_outdated, 1)` were formerly correct and had
gone out of date. Consistency was weaker: the registry and Medicare's
clinician directory disagreed on at least one variable for
`r pc(A$any_inconsistent_2026, 1)` of providers present in both,
concentrated in the finest geographic unit --
`r pc(A$zip_inconsistent, 1)` of postal codes but
`r pc(A$state_inconsistent, 1)` of practice states. Of providers whose
records disagreed in 2021, `r pc(A$unresolved_pct, 1)` still disagreed in
2026.

**CONCLUSION:** Practice state is the only geographic variable on which
these databases agree closely enough to support research. Analyses at
city or postal-code level rest on data that do not hold.

## Introduction

Research describing the midwifery workforce depends almost entirely on
federal administrative data [@bindman2013npi]. No national registry
records where a certified nurse-midwife practices; investigators
assemble the picture from records created for other purposes, each
capturing a practice address as an administrative by-product. Within
midwifery, identifying the workforce in these files is itself imperfect:
taxonomy alone undercounts certified midwives, and credential-field
recoding improves it [@vanderlaan2023midwives].

In May 2013 the Department of Health and Human Services Office of
Inspector General evaluated the two federal systems that establish who a
clinician is and where they practice [@oig2013]. Among the 987,266
providers listed in both, the systems disagreed on at least one variable
for `r pc(A$oig_any_benchmark, 0)` of providers, and practice location was
the least consistent variable at `r pc(A$oig_zip_benchmark, 1)`. That
evaluation had a gold standard -- a surveyed probability sample -- that
does not exist for this workforce: the certification board is
authoritative for the credential but records no address, and the only
records carrying an address are the records under examination. Two
primary sources do exist for other attributes: state boards of nursing
for licensure status, and the certification board for legal name.

This study had three objectives: to estimate the accuracy of federal
records describing midwives against independent primary sources; to
quantify completeness and pairwise consistency across federal and
commercial sources; and to determine which variables are fit for
geographic research on this workforce.

## Methods

### Cohort

The sampling frame was the American Midwifery Certification Board (AMCB)
public verification directory, the national roster of certified nurse-midwives and
certified midwives. Certificants were linked to NPPES by name and credential evidence, with linkage decisions
frozen before any analysis in this study was performed. Of `r cnt(linkage_total_n)` certification
records, `r cnt(linkage_matched_n)` (`r pc(linkage_matched_pct, 1)`) resolved
to a provider record, giving an analytic cohort of `r cnt(cohort_n)`
certificants once the nursing-taxonomy sensitivity tier is included.
Certification does not imply active practice: roughly a fifth of
certificants report no midwifery employment in the year before
recertification [@vanderlaan2023midwives], so absence from
billing-derived sources is expected for some members rather than
evidence of missing data. This study used only administrative and
publicly available records and was not human subjects research.

### Sources

`r N_word(A$sources_total_n)` record systems were examined (Table 1). NPPES
served as the reference standard, not because it is more accurate than the others but because it
assigns the identifier through which every other source is matched.
It instructs providers to update records within 30 days of a change but
neither enforces the update nor verifies that the submitted practice
address is where the provider works [@bindman2013npi].
`r N_word(A$sources_compared_n)` sources were compared pairwise against it.
Medicaid, specifically the Transformed Medicaid Statistical Information
System (T-MSIS), was carried as its own classification rather than as a percentage,
because it is the only source with a per-provider-year concordance already
constructed and because reducing concurrent multi-state enrollment to a single
state discards the categories of most interest.

```{r table-sources}
#| tbl-cap: "Table 1. Record systems examined, their custodian and role, the years each covers, and the public access point for each, sorted by custodian. The Transformed Medicaid Statistical Information System carries a per-provider-year concordance classification -- including concurrent enrollment in more than one state -- rather than a single state that could be set against the registry, so its consistency is analyzed separately rather than in Tables 3 and 4."
descr <- c(
  nppes = "National registry that assigns the National Provider Identifier; providers self-report practice address, credential, and taxonomy at enumeration and on update",
  dac_physician_compare = "CMS's public clinician directory, built from enrollment records and linked Medicare claims; the successor to Physician Compare",
  open_payments = "Industry-reported payments and transfers of value to covered recipients; nurse-midwives became reportable recipients in program year 2021",
  pecos_revalidation = "Medicare's enrollment, chain, and reassignment records; revalidation carries the practice address on file at enrollment",
  facility_affiliation_ccn = "CMS-published clinician-to-facility affiliation file distributed with the clinician directory",
  medicare_claims = "Part B carrier and Part D prescriber utilization files; a provider's state is the billing address on submitted claims",
  healthgrades = "Commercial provider directory aggregating self-reported and third-party practice information",
  doximity = "Commercial professional network whose member profiles form a provider directory",
  state_boards_of_nursing = "State licensure records; the primary source for license status and a verifying source for legal name",
  cms_ndh_fhir = "CMS's FHIR-based national provider directory consolidating directory data across programs")
descr["tmsis"] <- paste("Medicaid's transformed statistical system; provider",
  "enrollment carries a per-provider-year state concordance, and the 2018-2024",
  "spending release carries person-level billing activity")
descr["amcb"] <- paste("The certification board's roster of certified",
  "nurse-midwives; defines the cohort and is the primary source for the",
  "certified name")
if (!is.null(A$coverage_table)) {
  cv <- A$coverage_table
  cv$year <- as.integer(cv$year)
  span <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cv, cv$source), function(d) data.frame(
    source = d$source[1],
    years = if (length(unique(d$year)) == 1) as.character(unique(d$year)) else
      paste(range(d$year), collapse = "-"),
    n_years = length(unique(d$year)), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)))
  # Full system names only, no abbreviations; the prose introduces the
  # short forms at first use. The public access point for each is carried
  # in the table itself, so a reader can go to the record we read.
  label <- c(
    nppes = "National Plan and Provider Enumeration System",
    dac_physician_compare = "Doctors and Clinicians",
    open_payments = "Open Payments",
    pecos_revalidation = "Provider Enrollment, Chain and Ownership System",
    facility_affiliation_ccn = "Facility Affiliation",
    medicare_claims = "Medicare Part B and Part D claims",
    healthgrades = "Healthgrades",
    doximity = "Doximity",
    state_boards_of_nursing = "State boards of nursing",
    cms_ndh_fhir = "National Directory of Healthcare Providers and Services")
  access <- c(
    nppes = "https://download.cms.gov/nppes/NPI_Files.html",
    dac_physician_compare = "https://data.cms.gov/provider-data/topics/doctors-clinicians",
    open_payments = "https://openpaymentsdata.cms.gov/",
    pecos_revalidation = "https://data.cms.gov/provider-characteristics/medicare-provider-supplier-enrollment",
    facility_affiliation_ccn = "https://data.cms.gov/provider-data/topics/doctors-clinicians",
    medicare_claims = "https://data.cms.gov/summary-statistics-on-use-and-payments/medicare-provider-other-utilization-payment-data",
    healthgrades = "https://www.healthgrades.com/",
    doximity = "https://www.doximity.com/",
    state_boards_of_nursing = "https://data.colorado.gov/resource/7s5z-vewr, https://data.texas.gov/resource/jnzg-cr4w, https://data.wa.gov/resource/qxh8-f4bd, https://www.pals.pa.gov/",
    cms_ndh_fhir = "https://data.cms.gov/ndh")
  role <- ifelse(span$source == "nppes", "Reference standard", "Compared")
  out <- data.frame(
    `Record system` = label[span$source],
    Description = descr[span$source],
    Custodian = ifelse(span$source %in% c("healthgrades", "doximity"),
                       "Commercial",
                       ifelse(span$source == "state_boards_of_nursing",
                              "State", "Federal")),
    Role = role,
    `Years` = span$years,
    `Public access point` = access[span$source],
    check.names = FALSE)
  out <- rbind(out, data.frame(
    `Record system` =
      "Transformed Medicaid Statistical Information System",
    Description = descr["tmsis"],
    Custodian = "Federal",
    Role = "Multi-state concordance, analyzed separately",
    `Years` = A$medicaid_years,
    `Public access point` =
      "https://www.medicaid.gov/medicaid/data-systems/macbis/transformed-medicaid-statistical-information-system-t-msis/index.html",

  out <- rbind(out, data.frame(
    `Record system` = "American Midwifery Certification Board roster",
    Description = descr["amcb"],
    Custodian = "Certifying body", Role = "Cohort frame and primary source",

    `Public access point` = "https://www.amcbmidwife.org/",
    check.names = FALSE))
  out <- out[order(out$Custodian, out$`Record system`), ]
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "l", "l"))
}
```

### Design

We replicated the structure and the operational definitions of the Inspector
General's 2013 evaluation [@oig2013], implemented in a package written for
this purpose (`mysteryroster`). The replication preserves the evaluation's
three domains and its variable-level definitions, including its three-way
classification of inaccuracy, and departs from it in one respect: the
provider survey that supplied the Office of Inspector General's gold standard was
replaced by primary-source verification against records that exist
independently of the databases being evaluated.

### Accuracy, and the attributes for which it is estimable

Accuracy requires a record that can adjudicate the federal one. Two exist for
this cohort, covering licensure status and legal name; neither covers
practice location. Accuracy was therefore assessed for those two attributes
only, and the geographic variables are reported as agreement throughout.

*Licensure status* was verified against live state board of nursing records
obtained directly from each state's published licensure system. Three states
publish a machine-readable interface permitting verification of every record
(Colorado, Texas, and Washington); four further states were verified from
published files. Records that could not be matched to a board record were
classified as unresolved rather than inaccurate, and are reported both as a
point estimate among definitively resolved records and as sensitivity bounds
in which all unresolved records are assumed accurate or all inaccurate.

*Legal name* was verified against the certification board roster, which is the
primary source for a midwife's certified name.

Each inaccurate value was classified into the Office of Inspector General's three
subtypes: partially inaccurate, such as a misspelling or transposition;
formerly correct but no longer current; or never correct.

### Completeness

Completeness was the proportion of records eligible for a variable that
carried a populated value, distinguishing a field absent from the extract, a
record missing from the file, and a present record with a null value. Fields
not published by a given source were marked ineligible rather than counted as
incomplete.

### Consistency

Consistency was pairwise disagreement between two sources describing the same
provider. For sources with an annual vintage, providers were compared within
the same program year; for sources published only as a current snapshot, the
comparison was against the registry as it stood at extraction. Addresses were normalized following the
Office of Inspector General's appendix. Each source's observation window was declared
before analysis and every input verified for presence, schema and internal
program year, so a missing input failed the analysis rather than silently
narrowing it.

### Record age and resolution

To test whether disagreement reflected one record going stale, providers were
stratified by the elapsed time since the registry record was last updated, and
postal-code disagreement was computed within each stratum. To test whether
disagreements resolve, providers whose registry and Medicare enrollment
records disagreed in 2021 were followed through 2026 and classified by
whether either source adopted the other's value.

### Analysis

Proportions are reported with Wilson score intervals. The temporal trend in
agreement was estimated by weighted least squares with the number of
comparable providers as weights. All analyses were performed in R.

## Results

### What the sources cover

All `r n_word(A$sources_total_n)` record systems in Table 1 are reported here:
`r n_word(A$sources_compared_n)` compared pairwise against the reference
standard in Tables 3 and 4, the reference standard itself characterized for
completeness in Supplemental Table S1, and Medicaid classified separately below. No single
source covers the full 2007-2026 observation window (Supplemental Figure S1). Four of the `r n_word(A$sources_total_n)`
exist only as a current snapshot and cannot support any longitudinal claim.
Industry payment records begin in program year 2021, the first year in which
certified nurse-midwives were reportable covered recipients.



The structural problem underlying every comparison that follows is shown in
Supplemental Figure S2: the source that is authoritative for the credential holds no
address, and every source that holds an address is either self-reported or
derived from billing.



### Accuracy against independent primary sources

Accuracy is reported here only for licensure status and legal name, the two
attributes an outside record can adjudicate. Every geographic figure in this
paper is agreement, not accuracy, and the distinction is not a hedge: a
location on which two databases agree may be wrong in both, and nothing in
this design would detect it.

Where an independent primary source existed, the federal records were
accurate. Licensure status recorded in the national provider registry agreed
with live state board verification for
`r pc(A$nppes_license_3$pct_accurate, 2)` of
`r cnt(A$nppes_license_3$n_definitive)` definitively resolved records in the
three states with machine-readable verification, and for
`r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_accurate, 2)` of
`r cnt(A$nppes_license_7$n_definitive)` records across all seven states. The
Medicare enrollment system performed comparably, at
`r pc(A$pecos_license_3$pct_accurate, 2)` and
`r pc(A$pecos_license_7$pct_accurate, 2)` respectively.

The character of the errors matters more than their rate. Of the registry
records that were inaccurate on licensure status across seven states,
`r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_outdated, 1)` were formerly correct and had gone
out of date, `r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_typo, 1)` were partially inaccurate,
and `r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_never, 1)` had never been correct. In the
three machine-verified states, every inaccurate record was of the formerly
correct type. These databases are not being populated with wrong information;
they are being populated correctly and then not maintained.

Legal name, verified against the certification board roster, was the weaker
attribute: `r pc(A$nppes_name$pct_accurate, 2)` of
`r cnt(A$nppes_name$n_definitive)` registry records matched the certified
name, and `r pc(A$pecos_name$pct_accurate, 2)` of Medicare enrollment records.
Of the registry mismatches, `r pc(A$nppes_name$pct_typo, 1)` were partially
inaccurate rather than a different person, consistent with transcription and
with name change not being propagated.

```{r table-accuracy}
#| tbl-cap: "Table 2. Accuracy of the two provider attributes that have an independent primary source to be checked against: licensure status, verified against state board of nursing records, and legal name, verified against the certification board roster. Licensure status is shown at two verification depths -- the three states (Colorado, Texas, Washington) whose boards publish a live verification interface, where every record resolves definitively, and all seven states with obtainable board records, a set that adds four states verified from published files. Practice location, city, and postal code have no independent primary source, so Tables 3 and 4 report agreement between databases for them rather than verified accuracy."
if (!is.null(A$subtypes_table)) {
  tb <- A$subtypes_table
  # The artifact carries the systems by their acronyms; the manuscript names
  # them, per the journal's preference and so a reader need not decode them.
  db_label <- c("NPPES (2026)" = "National provider registry",
                "PECOS (2026)" = "Medicare enrollment system")
  out <- data.frame(
    `Database` = ifelse(tb$database %in% names(db_label),
                        db_label[tb$database], tb$database),
    `Primary source` = ifelse(grepl("Legal Name", tb$variable),
                              "Certification board roster",
                              "State boards of nursing"),
    `Attribute` = ifelse(grepl("Legal Name", tb$variable), "Legal name",
                         ifelse(grepl("3 API", tb$variable),
                                "Licensure status, 3 states with live board verification",
                                "Licensure status, all 7 states with board records")),
    `Resolved` = formatC(as.numeric(tb$n_definitive), format = "d",
                         big.mark = ","),
    `Accurate (%)` = sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(tb$pct_accurate_definitive)),
    `Errors formerly correct (%)` =
      sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(tb$pct_of_inaccurate_formerly)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

### Completeness

Completeness was high for the variables that matter geographically. In 2026,
practice state was populated for all but `r pc(A$nppes_state_incomplete, 2)`
of registry records and postal code for all but
`r pc(A$nppes_zip_incomplete, 2)`. Completeness was materially worse in the
public clinician directory for non-geographic fields, with telephone number
absent for `r pc(A$dac_phone_incomplete, 1)` and credential for
`r pc(A$dac_cred_incomplete, 1)` of records. One field is absent almost
entirely rather than partially -- the directly reported practice postal code
in the 2019 Medicare enrollment extract, null for 99.6% of records -- which is
why practice postal code for that source is read from the practice address
instead. For the geographic variables this study compares, completeness is
therefore not the limiting property of these data. Provider-years that leave
a billing source likewise almost always remain visible in the registry, so
source attrition is billing attrition rather than exit from the workforce
(Supplemental Table S4).


### Consistency between databases

Consistency, not accuracy, was the binding constraint. The registry and the
public clinician directory disagreed on at least one variable for
`r pc(A$any_inconsistent_2026, 1)` of `r cnt(A$any_overlap_2026)` providers
present in both, with a mean of
`r sprintf("%.2f", A$mean_inconsistent_vars)` disagreeing variables per
provider. The Office of Inspector General found `r pc(A$oig_any_benchmark, 1)` on the
same measure across all providers in 2011.

Disagreement was concentrated in the finest geographic unit. Practice postal
code disagreed for `r pc(A$zip_inconsistent, 1)` of providers, against the
Office of Inspector General's `r pc(A$oig_zip_benchmark, 1)`, while practice state
disagreed for only `r pc(A$state_inconsistent, 1)` (Figure 1, Table 3). The
same ordering held for every pair of sources examined.

![**Figure 1.** Disagreement by geographic granularity, against the Office of Inspector
General's 2011 benchmark. The dashed rule marks that benchmark: of the 987,266
providers listed in both federal systems in 2011, 88.6% had a practice-location
ZIP code that did not match between them.](`r fig("address_granularity_vs_oig_benchmark")`)

```{r table-consistency}
#| tbl-cap: "Table 3. Disagreement between the national provider registry and Medicare's public clinician directory, 2026, against the Office of Inspector General's 2011 benchmark."
if (!is.null(A$consistency_table)) {
  cs <- A$consistency_table
  cs <- cs[cs$year == "2026" & cs$source_a == "nppes" &
             cs$source_b == "dac", , drop = FALSE]
  label <- c(practice_zip5 = "Practice location (postal code)",
             phone10 = "Telephone number", credential = "Credential",
             full_name = "Full name", gender = "Gender",
             practice_state = "Practice state",
             specialty_code = "Specialty")
  cs <- cs[cs$attribute %in% names(label), , drop = FALSE]
  bm <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(cs$oig_2013_benchmark_inconsistent_pct))
  out <- data.frame(
    Variable = label[cs$attribute],
    `Compared` = formatC(as.numeric(cs$n_compared), format = "d",
                         big.mark = ","),
    `Office of Inspector General 2011 (%)` = ifelse(is.na(bm), "Not reported",
                                          sprintf("%.1f", bm)),
    `Midwifery cohort 2026 (%)` =
      sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(cs$pct_inconsistent_any_shared)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out[order(-as.numeric(cs$pct_inconsistent_any_shared)), ],
                         align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

### Record age and the direction of disagreement

Disagreement was not a simple function of staleness. Postal-code disagreement
was `r pc(A$stale_lt1, 1)` among records updated within the past year,
`r pc(A$stale_1_3, 1)` at one to three years, `r pc(A$stale_3_5, 1)` at three
to five years, and `r pc(A$stale_5p, 1)` beyond five years. The relationship
is U-shaped rather than monotonic: records updated most recently disagree
nearly as often as the most neglected ones, because a recent update generally
marks a recent move that the comparison source has not yet adopted.

Most disagreements never resolved. Of `r cnt(A$disagree_2021_n)` providers
whose registry and Medicare enrollment records disagreed in 2021,
`r pc(A$unresolved_pct, 1)` still disagreed in 2026. Where resolution did
occur it was slow, with a median of two to three years, and it ran in both
directions, so the disagreement cannot be attributed to a single lagging
system (Supplemental Table S3).

### Agreement over time

Agreement between the public clinician directory and the registry declined by
`r sprintf("%.2f", A$dac_slope_abs)` percentage points per year across
`r cnt(A$dac_years_n)` years (`r mw_pval(A$dac_p)`), so the decline in the most
recent year continues a trend rather than breaking a flat one (Supplemental Figure S3).
Industry payment records and Medicare enrollment records were flat across
their five and six years respectively.



```{r table-agreement}
#| tbl-cap: "Table 4. Agreement with the national provider registry, by source and year."
if (!is.null(A$agreement_table)) {
  ag <- A$agreement_table
  label <- c(dac_physician_compare = "Medicare clinician directory",
             open_payments = "Industry payment records",
             pecos_revalidation = "Medicare enrollment revalidation",
             facility_affiliation_ccn = "Hospital affiliation",
             medicare_claims = "Medicare claims (Parts B and D)",
             healthgrades = "Healthgrades", doximity = "Doximity",
             state_boards_of_nursing = "State boards of nursing",
             cms_ndh_fhir = "National directory of healthcare providers")
  out <- data.frame(
    Source = label[ag$source],
    Period = ifelse(grepl("^[0-9]{4}$", ag$year), ag$year,
                    sub(" \\(.*$", "", ag$year)),
    Basis = ifelse(ag$comparison_basis == "same_year", "Same year",
                   "Current snapshot"),
    Compared = formatC(as.numeric(ag$n_comparable), format = "d",
                       big.mark = ","),
    `Agree (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(ag$pct_agree)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r"))
}
```

### One Medicaid provider-year in six carries enrollment in more than one state at once

`r pc(A$medicaid_multistate_pct, 1)` of observed provider-years in the
Transformed Medicaid Statistical Information System (T-MSIS) involved
concurrent enrollment in more than one state. That is the rate at which the
single-state assumption every other comparison in this paper is forced to make
converts a correct record into an apparent error, and it is why T-MSIS was
classified per provider-year rather than reduced to a percentage.

Across `r A$medicaid_years` T-MSIS contributed
`r cnt(A$medicaid_total_n)` provider-years, of which
`r cnt(A$medicaid_observed_n)` carried an observable enrollment.
`r cnt(A$medicaid_concordant_n)` were concordant with the registry on a single
state and a further `r cnt(A$medicaid_multistate_concordant_n)` were
concordant through concurrent enrollment in more than one state, meaning the
registry's state was among those a midwife was enrolled in.

### Multi-state practice as a source of apparent disagreement

A portion of the disagreement between sources is not error. Scoring Medicaid
enrollment by whether a state is among those in which a midwife is
concurrently enrolled, rather than by whether it equals a single state
selected for her, raised agreement with the registry from
`r pc(A$medicaid_equality_pct, 1)` to `r pc(A$medicaid_membership_pct, 1)` on
the same `r cnt(A$medicaid_comparable_npi_years)` comparable provider-years.
No underlying record changed; only the question did. Commercial insurer
directories show the same mechanism: practice-address consistency rose
from 27.9% to 84.8% when only physicians practicing at a single location
were counted [@butala2023directories].

Multi-state enrollment is common rather than exceptional among midwives who
appear in Medicaid at all (Supplemental Figure S4).



Consistent with this, providers licensed in more than one state accounted for
a disproportionate share of cross-source disagreement (Supplemental Figure S5).
Unanimous agreement likewise falls as more sources report a state for the
same provider-year (Supplemental Table S2).



### Summary of what these data can support

Across all three domains, practice state behaved differently from every finer
geographic unit. It was essentially complete and the most consistent geographic
variable between every pair of sources examined -- though consistency is
agreement, not verified accuracy, since no primary source for practice location
exists. Practice postal code failed on consistency in roughly half of providers,
and that failure was not explained by update lag.

## Discussion

### Principal findings

Three findings organize the results. First, where an
independent record could adjudicate them, the federal systems were
accurate: licensure status verified against live state boards agreed in
the high nineties, and nearly every error was a formerly correct value
gone stale. Second, accuracy is not the
limiting property of these data -- consistency is. Correctly populated
records maintained on different schedules diverge, concentrated in the
finest geographic unit, replicating the
Office of Inspector General's ordering thirteen years later at similar
magnitudes. Third, disagreement mostly never resolves: of
providers whose registry and Medicare enrollment records disagreed in
2021, more than three quarters still disagreed in 2026, and resolution
ran in both directions -- not one system simply lagging another.

### Implications for workforce and access research

For workforce geography, these results draw a boundary through the
geographic hierarchy. Practice
state is the only unit on which the systems agree closely
enough to analyze as measured -- agreement, not verified accuracy, but
agreement this tight bounds how wrong any single source can be; postal
code is not. Half of providers disagreeing across two systems is too
large a fraction to analyze past, and the disagreement is not a lag
artifact that more time will heal. Licensure files show the same
hazard: one statewide study matched nurse-practitioner board addresses
to employment location in 5% of cases, and national provider-registry
addresses in 64% [@bell2018licensure].

Timeliness inverts a common assumption: where sources and the registry
disagreed across a transition, Medicare claims held the registry's
eventual value first in roughly three of five cases -- billing observes a
practice move before enumeration records it. The directories
researchers reach for are snapshots that cannot express
lag at all. A study needing *where she practises now* is better served by
claims-derived sources; one needing a *denominator*, by the registry's
completeness.

The same boundary applies to access-to-care inference. One Medicaid
provider-year in six carried concurrent enrollment in more than one
state; scoring that file by a single assigned state converted correct
records into apparent errors (agreement rose from
`r pc(A$medicaid_equality_pct, 1)` to `r pc(A$medicaid_membership_pct, 1)`
on identical data). For a workforce holding multiple state licenses,
"the practice state" is partly an artifact of the question asked.

### Comparison with previous studies

This study is a replication and an extension. The Office of Inspector
General's 2013 evaluation established the accuracy--completeness--consistency
framework, with a surveyed provider sample as the reference standard
[@oig2013]. Subsequent work comparing national physician sampling
frames, licensure records, and commercial directories documented
discrepancies in clinician addresses and specialty classifications
[@desroches2015sampling; @bell2018licensure]; a national comparison of five
major insurer directories found consistent practice-address information
for only 27.9% of physicians listed in more than one directory
[@butala2023directories]; in one re-survey, 44.8% of inaccurate listings
were still wrong months later [@haeder2024persistence]. Within
midwifery, taxonomy alone undercounts certified midwives and credential
fields improve identification, but that work addressed identification,
not the validity of practice addresses [@vanderlaan2023midwives].

Against this literature, the consistency findings replicate almost
exactly -- the same concentration in postal code, the same variable
ordering, and lower any-variable disagreement than the
`r pc(A$oig_any_benchmark, 0)` found across all providers in 2011, which
may reflect a smaller, more uniformly enumerated workforce rather than
improvement. The extension is a certification-defined cohort across
`r n_word(A$sources_total_n)` record systems, external verification where
a primary source exists, and longitudinal resolution data consistent with
the Office of Inspector General's finding that only 1.2% of location
disagreement was update lag: most disagreement persists for years.

### Strengths and limitations

The strengths are the cohort and the design: a certification-board frame
linked by a frozen, fully-accounted matching procedure, and comparisons
computed only within declared, content-verified observation windows --
every figure compares like with like.

The limitations bound what can be claimed. Four of the
`r n_word(A$sources_total_n)` record systems exist only as snapshots, so
their quality over time is not measurable.
Practice-location accuracy is not estimable: every geographic figure is
agreement, and a location on which two databases agree may be wrong in
both. Agreement comparisons weight by published records, so multi-record
sources count providers more than once. Agreement between sources sharing
upstream lineage -- Medicare Part B and Part D claims, Medicare
enrollment and the directory it feeds -- is within a family, not
independent corroboration.

### Conclusion

Federal and commercial databases agree on where a midwife practises at
the state level and disagree on the finer geography that access analysis
usually wants. The failures are failures of consistency, and structural:
records entered correctly but maintained on different
clocks diverge and mostly stay diverged. The registry is the most
complete source, billing-derived sources the most timely, and none is
both; study design should choose the property the question needs.

```{r table-completeness}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S1. Incomplete records among eligible fields, by source and year. The mailing-address ZIP is the provider's correspondence address, not their practice; the directly reported practice ZIP is the value the provider entered on their own enrollment record, distinct from the ZIP carried in the published practice address."
if (!is.null(A$completeness_table)) {
  ct <- A$completeness_table
  ct <- ct[as.numeric(ct$pct_incomplete_of_eligible) > 0, , drop = FALSE]
  var_label <- c(
    ssn_tin = "Social Security / taxpayer identification number",
    dob = "Date of birth",
    full_name = "Legal name",
    gender = "Sex / gender",
    specialty_code = "Specialty code",
    credential = "Credential",
    license_state = "License state",
    phone10 = "Telephone number",
    mailing_zip5 = "ZIP code of the provider's mailing (correspondence) address",
    practice_zip5_direct = "Practice ZIP code the provider reported on their own enrollment record",
    practice_zip5 = "Practice ZIP code taken from the practice address",
    practice_state = "Practice state")
  out <- data.frame(
    Year = ct$year,
    Source = c(nppes = "National provider registry",
               pecos = "Medicare enrollment",
               dac = "Medicare clinician directory")[ct$source],
    Variable = ifelse(ct$attribute %in% names(var_label),
                      var_label[ct$attribute], gsub("_", " ", ct$attribute)),
    `Records` = formatC(as.numeric(ct$n_records_present), format = "d",
                        big.mark = ","),
    `Incomplete (%)` = sprintf("%.2f",
                               as.numeric(ct$pct_incomplete_of_eligible)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out[order(out$Year, out$Source), ],
                         align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r"))
}
```

```{r table-source-count-agreement}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S2. Practice-state agreement as a function of the number of sources reporting a state in the same provider-year, in the style of the cross-directory comparison of Butala et al. Unanimous agreement requires every reporting source to record the same state; pairwise agreement is the share of source-pairs that agree. Unanimous agreement declines as more sources report, mirroring the dose-response reported for commercial insurer directories."
if (!is.null(A$source_count_table)) {
  sc <- A$source_count_table
  out <- data.frame(
    `Sources reporting a practice state` = sc$n_sources_reporting,
    `Provider-years` = formatC(as.numeric(sc$n_provider_years), format = "d",
                               big.mark = ","),
    `All sources agree (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
                                      as.numeric(sc$pct_unanimous_agreement)),
    `Source-pairs agreeing (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
                                          as.numeric(sc$pct_pairwise_agreement)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

```{r table-resolution-disposition}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S3. Disposition of provider-years on which a source and the national provider registry held discordant practice states at the base year, measured at the next observation, in the style of the follow-up taxonomy of Haeder and Zhu. 'Source adopted registry' and 'registry adopted source' are the two directions of resolution; 'both moved' means both records changed to a third value. Columns may not sum to 100 where a provider-year left observation."
if (!is.null(A$resolution_table)) {
  rs <- A$resolution_table
  label <- c(pecos_revalidation = "Medicare enrollment revalidation",
             medicare_part_b = "Medicare Part B claims",
             medicare_part_d = "Medicare Part D claims",
             open_payments = "Industry payment records",
             medicaid_enrollment = "Medicaid enrollment (T-MSIS)")[rs$source_b]
  out <- data.frame(
    Source = ifelse(is.na(label), rs$source_b, label),
    `Base year` = rs$base_year,
    `Discordant (n)` = formatC(as.numeric(rs$n_discordant_at_t), format = "d",
                               big.mark = ","),
    `Still discordant (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      as.numeric(rs$persistent_discordant_at_t1_pct)),
    `Source adopted registry (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      as.numeric(rs$b_adopts_a_at_t1_pct)),
    `Registry adopted source (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      as.numeric(rs$a_reverts_to_b_at_t1_pct)),
    `Both moved (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      100 * as.numeric(rs$both_move_together_at_t1) /
        as.numeric(rs$n_discordant_at_t)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

```{r table-persistence-denominators}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S4. Where a provider-year goes by the following year, aggregated across each source's observed window. A provider who leaves a billing source is rarely leaving the workforce: most remain visible in the national provider registry, so source attrition is billing attrition rather than exit from practice. Same-state and different-state shares are computed among provider-years re-observed in the same source; the leavers' registry-visibility share is computed among provider-years absent from the source at the next observation. The registry itself is omitted because persistence in it and visibility in it cannot be distinguished."
if (!is.null(A$persistence_table)) {
  ps <- A$persistence_table
  ps <- ps[ps$source != "nppes", , drop = FALSE]
  label <- c(nppes = "National provider registry",
             pecos_revalidation = "Medicare enrollment revalidation",
             medicare_claims = "Medicare claims (Parts B and D)",
             medicaid_enrollment = "Medicaid enrollment (T-MSIS)",
             open_payments = "Industry payment records")[ps$source]
  out <- data.frame(
    Source = ifelse(is.na(label), ps$source, label),
    `Observed (n)` = formatC(ps$n_observed, format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    `In source next year (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      100 * ps$n_followed_source / ps$n_observed),
    `Same state (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      100 * ps$n_same_state / ps$n_followed_source),
    `Different state (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      100 * ps$n_changed_state / ps$n_followed_source),
    `Left source (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      100 * ps$n_lost_from_source / ps$n_observed),
    `Leavers still in registry (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      100 * ps$n_lost_source_but_in_nppes / ps$n_lost_from_source),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out[order(-ps$n_observed), ],
                         align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```
